relationship: Parallel lists of nations to be displaced
rationale: Both name the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites as peoples encountered in the land, while Exodus describes the angel going ahead.

relationship: Repeated promise concerning stronger nations
rationale: Both describe the Lord removing nations greater and mightier than Israel so that Israel may inherit, explicitly distinguishing divine agency from superior Israelite numbers.

relationship: Repeated prohibition of covenants with the nations
rationale: Both prohibit making a covenant with the land's inhabitants; Exodus also names their gods, while this verse adds the stated destruction and no-mercy instructions.

relationship: Displacement promise and covenant warning
rationale: Exodus announces driving out the named nations and warns against covenanting with their inhabitants, corresponding to the paired delivery and no-covenant clauses here.

relationship: Parallel intermarriage prohibitions
rationale: Both prohibit exchanging daughters and sons in marriage with the nations, while Exodus explicitly connects these marriages with leading sons into the nations' worship.

relationship: Marriage warning and later farewell admonition
rationale: Joshua warns against intermarrying and mingling with remaining nations and predicts their becoming snares, corresponding to Deuteronomy's marriage prohibition and its surrounding apostasy warning.

relationship: Stated danger of marriage leading to other gods
rationale: Both describe family relationships leading sons toward the nations' gods; Deuteronomy adds the Lord's anger and threatened rapid destruction as consequences.

relationship: Other-god worship and threatened divine anger
rationale: Both warn against following surrounding gods and describe the Lord's anger bringing destruction, providing the particular covenant danger behind this marriage warning.

relationship: Parallel destruction of cult objects
rationale: Both enumerate tearing down altars, breaking pillars, cutting sacred groves and burning carved images, preserving the specific actions and objects in each instruction.

relationship: Related refusal and demolition of foreign worship
rationale: Exodus prohibits bowing to or serving the gods and commands overthrowing their installations and pillars; Deuteronomy gives a fuller list including groves and burned images.

relationship: Repeated holy and chosen possession description
rationale: Both identify Israel as holy to the Lord and chosen as His possession from the nations upon earth, placing the same identity formula within different instructions.

relationship: Covenant possession and holy people
rationale: Exodus associates obedience to the covenant with being the Lord's treasured people and holy nation; Deuteronomy uses holy-people and chosen-possession language to ground its commands.

relationship: Same-chapter rejected and stated grounds of election
rationale: Israel's numbers are rejected as the reason for the Lord's choice; the following verse gives His love and faithfulness to the ancestral oath as the reasons.

relationship: Related descriptions of the Lord's preferential choice
rationale: Both describe the Lord preferring and choosing Israel, with chapter10 explicitly connecting the choice of descendants to love for their fathers rather than numerical superiority.

relationship: Ancestral pledge and Egyptian deliverance
rationale: Both recall mighty-hand deliverance from Egyptian slavery and connect departure with the land sworn to the fathers; this verse expressly identifies divine love as its motive.

relationship: Faithfulness to the oath sworn to the fathers
rationale: Both ground divine mercy or deliverance in the covenant sworn to the fathers, while chapter4 applies that faithfulness to Israel's future distress and return.

relationship: Mercy associated with loving and keeping instruction
rationale: Both connect the Lord's mercy with those who love Him and keep His commandments, while retaining the distinct formulations of thousands and a thousand generations.

relationship: Divine faithfulness and mercy in self-description
rationale: Exodus proclaims the Lord merciful and true, showing mercy to thousands; Deuteronomy describes Him as the faithful God who keeps covenant and mercy across generations.

relationship: Recompense concerning those who hate the Lord
rationale: Both describe divine repayment in relation to hatred of the Lord; Exodus's intergenerational wording differs from Deuteronomy's direct and undelayed recompense to the hater.

relationship: Same-chapter contrasting responses to love and hatred
rationale: The repayment of those who hate the Lord is set beside covenant mercy for those who love Him and keep His commands, preserving both sides of the contrast.

relationship: Repeated categories of instruction to be kept
rationale: Both combine commandments, ordinances and judgments with the requirement to do them; chapter6 additionally specifies their teaching and observance across succeeding generations in the land.

relationship: Same-chapter covenant mercy stated and condition applied
rationale: The promised keeping of covenant and mercy upon hearing and doing the ordinances applies the earlier description of God keeping covenant mercy with command-keeping lovers.

relationship: Obedience, promised blessings and covenant establishment
rationale: Both introduce agricultural and population blessings through obedience, and both explicitly connect those blessings with maintaining or establishing the Lord's covenant.

relationship: Related lists of agricultural covenant provision
rationale: Both name grain, wine, oil and cattle provision within obedient covenant life; this verse additionally names multiplication and offspring, while chapter11 specifies rain and pasture.

relationship: Parallel agricultural and population blessings
rationale: Leviticus promises seasonal rain, produce, satisfied eating and multiplication under obedience; Deuteronomy specifies human offspring, livestock increase and grain, wine and oil within that blessing pattern.

relationship: Parallel promise against barrenness
rationale: Both promise absence of barrenness in the land; Deuteronomy expressly includes male and female persons and cattle, while Exodus also speaks of fulfilled days.

relationship: Disease promise explicitly recalling Egypt
rationale: Both promise that Egyptian diseases will not be laid upon obedient Israel; Deuteronomy also speaks of removing infirmity and placing those diseases upon Israel's haters.

relationship: Service and promised removal of sickness
rationale: Exodus connects serving the Lord with blessed food and water and sickness turned away; Deuteronomy similarly promises removal of infirmity within its obedient covenant blessing.

relationship: Foreign worship described as a snare
rationale: Both warn that serving the nations' gods becomes a snare or stumbling block, connecting the restriction on their presence or spoil with fidelity to the Lord.

relationship: Same-chapter spoil warning and prohibited cult property
rationale: The command concerning the nations' spoil is limited by the later specific prohibition on taking precious metals from idols or bringing devoted abominations into the house.

relationship: Same-chapter fearful numerical calculation and answer
rationale: The imagined objection that the nation is more numerous receives an explicit answer: do not fear, but remember the Lord's witnessed Egyptian signs and deliverance.

relationship: Earlier numerical fear and countervailing divine assurance
rationale: The earlier report of stronger, numerous people and great cities caused fear; Moses answered that the Lord would fight as He had in Egypt, matching the argument here.

relationship: Egyptian deliverance used against fear of enemies
rationale: Both counter fear of the land's opponents by recalling what the Lord did in Egypt, with chapter1 explicitly stating that He will fight before Israel.

relationship: Repeated eyewitness recital of Egyptian trials and signs
rationale: Both address hearers who saw the Egyptian deeds, calling them great trials, signs and wonders; this verse additionally applies their remembrance to the feared nations.

relationship: Parallel promise of hornets preceding displacement
rationale: Both explicitly promise hornets as an agent of driving out the nations, with Deuteronomy emphasizing remaining and hiding people and Exodus naming particular nations.

relationship: Related divine-presence reassurance in entry commands
rationale: Deuteronomy's assurance that the great and mighty God is in Israel's midst corresponds to Joshua's assurance that the Lord is with him wherever he goes; their exact warning language differs.

relationship: Gradual displacement and wild-animal rationale
rationale: Both specify little-by-little removal instead of immediate clearing and expressly connect the gradual pace with avoiding desolation and multiplication of wild beasts.

relationship: Parallel delivery of the inhabitants into Israel's hands
rationale: Both promise delivery of the land's inhabitants into Israel's hands; Exodus additionally gives territorial borders and speaks of casting them out, while Deuteronomy speaks of destruction.

relationship: No opponent standing and subsequent conquest summary
rationale: Joshua describes great strong nations destroyed and no one standing against Israel, corresponding to the promise that no one will stand until the named opponents are destroyed.

relationship: Repeated assurance that none will withstand Israel
rationale: Both explicitly state that none will stand before Israel, while this verse additionally speaks of kings and erased names and chapter11 names dread upon the land.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated burning of carved images
rationale: The later ban on coveting idol metals repeats the earlier command to burn carved images, giving a particular restriction on appropriating their precious materials.

relationship: Same-chapter household ban following the idol-metal warning
rationale: The ban on bringing an abomination home follows the prohibition on taking idol silver or gold, extending the warning to the household and identifying the property as devoted.

relationship: Repeated obedience, life, multiplication and inheritance sequence
rationale: Both command performance of the delivered instruction so that Israel may live, multiply and enter to inherit the land given by the God of the fathers.

relationship: Repeated command-keeping purpose and ancestral land oath
rationale: Both connect keeping all the commandments with living, multiplying and entering the land, explicitly relating that inheritance to the Lord's oath to the fathers.

relationship: Wilderness provision as a test of obedience
rationale: Both describe wilderness testing to disclose whether Israel will keep divine instruction; Exodus specifically places the test in the daily gathering of heaven's bread.

relationship: Explicit citation of life beyond bread alone
rationale: Jesus answers the bread-making temptation with the written statement that human life depends on every word proceeding through God's mouth, reproducing the key teaching of this verse.

relationship: Shorter explicit citation in the temptation account
rationale: Luke records Jesus replying that a human shall not live on bread alone; the saved text stops there and does not reproduce Deuteronomy's following every-word clause.

relationship: Unknown wilderness food identified as divine bread
rationale: Both describe previously unfamiliar wilderness food; Exodus records the people's question and Moses' identification of it as bread given by the Lord, while Deuteronomy explains its lesson.

relationship: Forty-year preservation with different bodily details
rationale: Both affirm that garments did not wear out during forty wilderness years; chapter8 names feet not becoming calloused, whereas chapter29 names sandals not wearing away.

relationship: Father-and-son imagery for wilderness dealings
rationale: Both compare the Lord's treatment of Israel with a man's treatment of his son, distinguishing chapter1's nurturing image from this verse's explicit chastening.

relationship: Divine discipline explained through fatherhood
rationale: Both use a father disciplining a son to explain divine chastening; Hebrews expands this into submission and benefit, without claiming that its accompanying quotation is from Deuteronomy.

relationship: Fear, walking and command keeping combined
rationale: Both require fearing the Lord, walking in His ways and keeping His commandments; chapter10 also expressly includes wholehearted love and service for Israel's good.

relationship: Related descriptions of the land's water and care
rationale: Chapter8 describes torrents and springs across plains and hills; chapter11 describes hills and plains drinking heaven's rain and receiving the Lord's continuing care, preserving the distinct water sources.

relationship: Land produce and promised harvest provision
rationale: The named wheat, barley, vines and olive oil correspond to the later promise of grain, wine and oil through seasonal rain, without equating the two crop lists completely.

relationship: Same-chapter completion of the good-land description
rationale: Bread without poverty, lack of nothing and mineral-bearing terrain complete the preceding description of abundant water and crops, distinguishing the several resources named in the land encomium.

relationship: Same-chapter satisfied eating and contrasting responses
rationale: The command to bless after eating in the good land is contrasted with the ensuing danger that filled tables, good houses and increasing possessions lead to forgetting the giver.

relationship: Parallel warning against forgetting amid prosperity
rationale: Both warn against forgetting the Lord after receiving houses and satisfying food in the promised land, explicitly linking remembered identity with deliverance from Egyptian bondage.

relationship: Shared houses, satisfied eating and remembrance warning
rationale: Both combine good houses and eating to fullness with a warning against forgetting the Lord; chapter6 additionally specifies that the houses were not built by the recipients.

relationship: Same-chapter multiplied possessions and their source
rationale: The increase of herds, flocks, silver and gold provides the concrete wealth later attributed wrongly to one's own power and correctly to strength given by the Lord.

relationship: Repeated danger of forgetting the deliverer from bondage
rationale: Both explicitly identify the forgotten Lord as the One who brought Israel out of Egypt and the house of bondage; this verse particularly names a lifted-up heart.

relationship: Rock-water provision in the wilderness
rationale: The recital of water brought from sheer rock corresponds to the command to strike the Horeb rock and the resulting drinking water, retaining the narrative's explicit setting.

relationship: Serpents within the wilderness journey
rationale: The fearful wilderness description includes biting serpents; Numbers narrates a particular serpent judgment and subsequent remedy, without claiming that every wilderness serpent mentioned here belongs to that episode.

relationship: Manna and testing obedience
rationale: Both connect the wilderness bread with divine testing; Exodus states the question of walking in the law, while Deuteronomy adds humbling and intended later good.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated humbling, testing and manna explanation
rationale: This verse resumes the preceding account of wilderness humbling, testing and unfamiliar manna, now explicitly adding the purpose of doing good in the latter days.

relationship: Same-chapter false and corrected accounts of wealth
rationale: The inner claim that one's own strength gained wealth is answered by remembering the Lord as the giver of strength to gain it and keeper of the ancestral covenant.

relationship: Same-chapter divine gift correcting self-attribution
rationale: The statement that the Lord gives strength to gain wealth directly corrects the preceding assertion that one's own hand alone obtained the great wealth.

relationship: Idolatry, heaven-and-earth witness and threatened perishing
rationale: Both invoke heaven and earth as witnesses against Israel and announce perishing in connection with idolatry; chapter4 specifically describes making a graven likeness after long residence.

relationship: Repeated prohibition of other-god allegiance
rationale: Both warn against following the nations' gods and connect the action with threatened destruction, while this verse expressly includes forgetting, serving and bowing down.

relationship: Israel's warning measured against the displaced nations
rationale: The threat that Israel will perish like displaced nations recalls the earlier destruction and other-god warnings; the comparison makes obedience, rather than possession alone, decisive.

relationship: Repeated report of great nations and heaven-high walls
rationale: Both describe great, numerous or stronger peoples and cities walled up to heaven, while the earlier passage reports the words that caused the hearers' hearts to fail.

relationship: Tall opponents and earlier report of giants
rationale: Chapter9 names the tall sons of Anak, while the earlier report describes sons of giants among the intimidating inhabitants; the comparison preserves the differing identification language.

relationship: Repeated consuming-fire description in different settings
rationale: Both call the Lord a consuming fire; chapter4 uses the image with jealousy and an idol warning, while chapter9 applies it to divine action against the land's opponents.

relationship: Divine action preceding Israel against the opponents
rationale: Both state that the Lord goes before Israel and acts against the enemies; chapter1 speaks of fighting, while chapter9 describes consuming fire and destruction.

relationship: Land transfer related to the inhabitants' sins
rationale: Deuteronomy denies Israelite righteousness as the cause and names the nations' ungodliness; Genesis explains delayed return through the Amorites' sins not yet being filled up.

relationship: Same-chapter denial of meritorious grounds repeated
rationale: The warning against saying one's righteous deeds secured the land is expanded by the following denial of righteousness or heart-holiness and the description of Israel as stiff-necked.

relationship: Ancestral covenant and explicitly named promised peoples
rationale: Genesis records the covenant giving Abram's seed land occupied by named peoples; Deuteronomy relates inheritance to establishing the oath sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob rather than Israel's righteousness.

relationship: Ancestral oath distinguished from Israel's superiority
rationale: Both reject an Israelite basis for boasting and affirm the Lord's ancestral oath, with chapter7 rejecting superior numbers and chapter9 rejecting righteous deeds or heart-holiness.

relationship: Stiff-necked people and Moses' appeal for forgiveness
rationale: Both describe Israel as stiff-necked; in Exodus Moses nevertheless asks the Lord to accompany and forgive them, matching the denial that their righteousness earned the land.

relationship: Same-chapter summary of provocation and specified episodes
rationale: The general charge of continuing wilderness disobedience is later illustrated by Burning, Testing, Graves of Desire and the refused Kadesh-barnea entry instruction.

relationship: Horeb provocation and threatened destruction
rationale: The recital of anger and threatened destruction corresponds to the Lord's report of the molten calf and His announced intention to destroy the people; the actual Exodus sequence omits32:9.

relationship: Mountain ascent for tablets and forty-day stay
rationale: Both describe Moses ascending to receive stone tablets and remaining forty days and nights; Deuteronomy also expressly states his abstention from bread and water.

relationship: Forty-day fast in a distinct tablet episode
rationale: Both explicitly mention forty days and nights without bread or water; Exodus34 concerns the renewed covenant tablets, whereas Deuteronomy here recalls the initial reception before the calf.

relationship: Stone tablets written with God's finger
rationale: Both identify the two stone tablets as written with God's finger; Deuteronomy further connects their words with the public mountain assembly.

relationship: Forty-day mountain period before tablet reception
rationale: The receipt of the tablets after forty days and nights corresponds to Exodus's account of Moses remaining within the cloud on the mountain for that duration.

relationship: Divine command to descend because of the calf
rationale: Both have the Lord command Moses to descend quickly because the people brought from Egypt have transgressed the commanded way and made a molten calf or image.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated stiff-necked description
rationale: The reported divine description of the people as stiff-necked repeats the earlier description used to deny their righteous deeds as the ground of receiving the land.

relationship: Threatened destruction and a new nation from Moses
rationale: Both announce destruction of the people and a replacement nation made from Moses; Deuteronomy additionally specifies erased names and greater strength and numbers.

relationship: Moses' descent with tablets in his hands
rationale: Both recount Moses turning and descending from the mountain carrying two tablets; Deuteronomy mentions the burning mountain and Exodus additionally describes writing on both sides.

relationship: Moses sees the calf on approaching the people
rationale: Both narrate Moses personally seeing the calf or molten image after descending; Exodus also names the dancing and the anger preceding the tablets' destruction.

relationship: Breaking of the two tablets
rationale: Both recount Moses casting the two tablets from his hands and breaking them; Deuteronomy stresses the people's sight of it and Exodus locates it at the mountain's foot.

relationship: Renewed intercession after the calf sin
rationale: Both describe Moses returning to plead over the people's great sin; Deuteronomy gives the forty-day fast, while Exodus records the appeal for forgiveness and offered erasure from the book.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated duration of intercession
rationale: Both state forty days and forty nights of entreaty in response to the sin and threatened destruction; verse18 additionally explicitly describes fasting from bread and water.

relationship: Intercession heard amid threatened judgment
rationale: Deuteronomy affirms that the Lord heard Moses at that time; Exodus describes the Lord being appeased concerning the calamity He had announced against His people.

relationship: Aaron's particular involvement in the calf offense
rationale: Deuteronomy reports anger against Aaron and prayer for him; Exodus supplies Moses' accusation and Aaron's explanation, without itself stating the separate prayer recorded here.

relationship: Destruction and dispersal of the calf with different details
rationale: Both describe burning and finely grinding the calf and dispersing the residue into water; Deuteronomy names the mountain torrent, while Exodus adds making Israel drink it.

relationship: Named Burning provocation and its narrative
rationale: The recital names Burning among the provocations; Numbers explains that name through the fire kindled after grumbling and quenched when Moses prayed.

relationship: Named Testing provocation and water dispute
rationale: The recital names Testing; Exodus identifies Testing and Reviling after the people's thirsty dispute and question whether the Lord was among them.

relationship: Related craving-burial episode with distinct place-name forms
rationale: Deuteronomy names Graves of Desire among provocations; Numbers narrates quail, plague and burials at Graves of Craving, preserving the two supplied name forms rather than replacing either.

relationship: Kadesh-barnea command and refusal retold
rationale: Both locate the entry instruction at Kadesh-barnea and record the command to ascend and inherit followed by refusal to go up and disobedience to the Lord's word.

relationship: Repeated characterization as failure to trust
rationale: The accusation of not believing the Lord at the land-entry refusal corresponds to the earlier statement that the people did not trust Him in that matter.

relationship: Same-chapter encompassing charge of disobedience
rationale: Both frame the particular episodes with a broad accusation of continuing disobedience, preserving their different starting formulations of departure from Egypt and the Lord's becoming known.

relationship: Same-chapter intercession repeated against threatened destruction
rationale: The forty-day entreaty because of threatened destruction resumes the earlier forty-day fast and fear of divine wrath, where Moses states that the Lord heard him.

relationship: Intercession appeals to the delivered people
rationale: Both plead for the people on the ground that the Lord brought them out of Egypt by great strength and an uplifted arm; Deuteronomy expands the invocation and redemption wording.

relationship: Intercession appeals to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
rationale: Both ask the Lord to remember the named patriarchal servants and His self-sworn pledge, while Deuteronomy also pleads against considering the people's hardness and sins.

relationship: Intercession invokes possible Egyptian interpretation
rationale: Both plead against the former land's inhabitants interpreting the departure as an intention to kill Israel; Deuteronomy additionally names alleged inability to bring them into the promised land.

relationship: Divine ownership and Egyptian deliverance in the plea
rationale: Both call Israel the Lord's people and appeal to their mighty deliverance from Egypt; Deuteronomy also calls them His inheritance in this concluding appeal.

relationship: Same-chapter people-and-portion appeal frames the prayer
rationale: The closing identification as God's people and inheritance repeats the opening appeal for His redeemed people and portion, with great strength and uplifted arm recurring in both.

relationship: Replacement-tablet command with added ark instruction
rationale: Both command hewing two stone tablets like the broken first pair and ascending the mountain; Deuteronomy additionally includes making a wooden ark in this command.

relationship: Promise to rewrite the broken tablets' words
rationale: Both promise writing the former words upon replacement stone tablets; Deuteronomy additionally commands placing them in the ark, which Exodus's replacement command does not mention.

relationship: Tablets and the ark's instructed contents
rationale: The command to put the rewritten tablets in the ark corresponds to Exodus's instruction to place the given testimonies inside the ark, retaining the differing content descriptions.

relationship: Moses hews replacement tablets and ascends
rationale: Both narrate Moses cutting two tablets like the first and ascending with them; Deuteronomy also describes the decay-resistant wooden ark he made.

relationship: Ark material in recital and construction instruction
rationale: Both specify an ark of decay-resistant wood; Exodus supplies the testimony-ark dimensions and later gold instructions, while Deuteronomy's recital here names the wood without those details.

relationship: Ten words on the renewed covenant tablets
rationale: Both identify the renewed tablet contents as the ten words; Deuteronomy explicitly attributes the writing to the Lord and recalls the mountain and fire, preserving Exodus's own narration.

relationship: Placement corresponding to the ark-content command
rationale: Deuteronomy narrates Moses placing the tablets in the ark as commanded; Exodus gives the instruction to place the divinely given testimonies inside it.

relationship: Aaron's death and Eleazar's succession with distinct locations
rationale: Both recount Aaron's death and Eleazar's succeeding priestly role; Deuteronomy locates the death at Misadai, whereas Numbers specifies Mount Hor, without harmonizing the locations.

relationship: Shared Gadgad-to-Jotbathah itinerary segment
rationale: Both give departure from Gadgad toward Jotbathah; Numbers calls the former Mount Gadgad and continues onward to Abronah, while Deuteronomy characterizes Jotbathah by flowing torrents.

relationship: Levitical choice for standing, ministry and blessing
rationale: Deuteronomy10 sets apart the tribe of Levi, while chapter18 speaks of the chosen priestly minister and his sons; both name standing, ministry and blessing, with ark-bearing additionally stated here.

relationship: Ark-bearing tribe and particular carrying assignment
rationale: Deuteronomy describes Levi's separation to bear the covenant ark; Numbers assigns covered holy-object carrying specifically to Kohath's sons after the priests prepare them, preserving that narrower role.

relationship: Repeated Levitical inheritance formula
rationale: Both deny Levi a portion or inheritance among the brethren and state that the Lord is his inheritance, with chapter18 also naming offerings as their food inheritance.

relationship: No territorial inheritance and divine provision
rationale: Numbers directly tells Aaron that the Lord is his inheritance and separately denies territorial inheritance to Levites while assigning tithes; Deuteronomy applies its inheritance statement to Levites.

relationship: Renewed forty-day stay and heard intercession
rationale: Both mention forty days and nights and the Lord hearing Moses amid threatened destruction; chapter9 expressly adds fasting and fear of the Lord's wrath.

relationship: Forty-day renewed-tablet mountain stay
rationale: Both describe Moses remaining before the Lord forty days and nights in the renewed-tablet setting; Exodus additionally names fasting and the covenant's ten words.

relationship: Renewed instruction to lead the people onward
rationale: Both follow the calf crisis with a command for Moses to lead the people to the announced destination; Deuteronomy explicitly identifies entry and ancestral sworn inheritance.

relationship: Wholehearted love within the required allegiance
rationale: Both require love for the Lord with all heart and soul; chapter6 also says all strength, while this verse combines love with fear, walking and service.

relationship: Fear and service in repeated allegiance instructions
rationale: Both require fearing and serving the Lord; chapter6 additionally commands cleaving and swearing by His name, while chapter10 expressly calls for wholehearted love and walking in His ways.

relationship: Command keeping and the stated good of Israel
rationale: Both connect keeping divine ordinances with Israel's wellbeing, with chapter6 additionally stating fear of the Lord and continued life as purposes of that instruction.

relationship: Universal divine ownership beside Israel's special covenant
rationale: Deuteronomy attributes heaven and earth with their contents to the Lord; Exodus likewise says all the earth is His while describing Israel's particular covenant possession.

relationship: Love and choice linked to the fathers
rationale: Both connect Israel's election with divine love and the fathers, while chapter7 explicitly rejects superior population as the reason and recalls the ancestral oath.

relationship: Hard heart command answers the stiff-necked diagnosis
rationale: The command to circumcise heart-hardness and cease stiffening the neck answers the earlier description of Israel as stiff-necked, without reducing the metaphor to a physical procedure.

relationship: Divine impartiality and corresponding judicial prohibitions
rationale: The Lord is described as taking neither partiality nor a bribe; the later instruction forbids those same practices in Israel's judges, naming the distortion bribery causes.

relationship: Divine care and communal provision for vulnerable groups
rationale: The Lord executes judgment for sojourner, orphan and widow and gives the sojourner food and clothing; chapter24 requires their just treatment and access to harvest produce.

relationship: Love for resident foreigners grounded in Egyptian experience
rationale: Both command love for the resident foreigner or sojourner and give Israel's own foreign residence in Egypt as the explicit reason, with Leviticus also prohibiting oppression.

relationship: Egyptian sojourning grounds treatment of foreigners
rationale: Both ground the treatment of a resident foreigner in Israel's own residence in Egypt, with Deuteronomy commanding love and Exodus prohibiting ill-treatment and affliction.

relationship: Repeated fear, service, cleaving and oath formula
rationale: Both command fearing the Lord, serving Him, cleaving to Him and swearing by His name, retaining this edition's complete four-part instruction.

relationship: Witnessed divine works as grounds for allegiance
rationale: The great glorious deeds seen by Israel's eyes are specified in the following recital of Egyptian signs, sea deliverance and wilderness events witnessed by the addressed hearers.

relationship: Star-multitude pledge and claimed multiplication
rationale: Genesis promises Abram descendants like the stars he cannot count; Deuteronomy describes the people's present multitude by that same star image after their Egyptian sojourn.

relationship: Egyptian household totals preserved as differing accounts
rationale: Deuteronomy says the fathers entered Egypt with seventy souls; Genesis distinguishes sixty-six direct entrants and a household total of seventy-five, so no numerical equivalence is asserted.
